claims.text: Substrate thermal conductivity governs interfacial heat dissipation in approximately 50 nm FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA films during magnetic-cooling cycles.
A high-thermal-conductivity substrate will enhance heat transfer away from the HEA film.
Enhanced heat transfer will accelerate phase-transformation kinetics during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Enhanced heat transfer will make the phase transformation more spatially uniform.
A faster cooling rate will reduce residence time in nonequilibrium states.
Reduced residence time in nonequilibrium states will reduce magnetic hysteresis.
Reduced residence time in nonequilibrium states will improve the magnetocaloric response.
A low-thermal-conductivity substrate will impede heat extraction from the film.
Impeded heat extraction will produce slower transformation kinetics.
Slower transformation kinetics will produce greater hysteresis.
Slower transformation kinetics will diminish the magnetocaloric effect.
Films on sapphire will exhibit a larger isothermal entropy change than otherwise identical films on borosilicate glass.
Films on sapphire will exhibit less magnetic hysteresis than otherwise identical films on borosilicate glass.
Sapphire functions as the high-thermal-conductivity substrate and borosilicate glass as the low-thermal-conductivity substrate in the proposed comparison.
Substrate-induced strain may influence the magnetocaloric response independently of heat transfer.
Substrate-dependent microstructural variations may influence the magnetocaloric response independently of heat transfer.
The proposed effect is expected near the phase-transformation temperature region for films around 50 nm thick under low applied fields.
The substrate effect can be isolated only if films on the two substrates have comparable microstructural quality and strain differences are accounted for.
